metadata.title: Content and Format of Composition Statement and Corresponding Statement of Ingredients in Labeling in NDAs and ANDAs
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics

candidates.statement: In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities. 44 Instead, guidances describe the Agency’s current thinking on a topic and should be viewed only 45 as recommendations, unless specific regulatory or statutory requirements are cited. The use of 46 the word should in Agency guidance means that something is suggested or recommended, but 47 not required. 48

candidates.statement: Section 505(j) of the FD&C Act, together with its implementing regulations, generally requires 60 that an ANDA must contain information to demonstrate that the proposed drug product and the 61 applicable reference listed drug (RLD) are the same with respect to active ingredient(s), dosage 62 form, route of administration, strength, previously approved conditions of use, and, with certain 63 exceptions, labeling. 7 An ANDA must also include sufficient information to demonstrate that 64 the proposed drug product is bioequivalent to the RLD 8 and must demonstrate that the methods 65 used in, or facilities and controls used for, the manufacture, processing, and packing of the drug 66 are adequate to assure and preserve its identity, strength, quality, and purity. 9 An ANDA 67
candidates.context: Section 505(b)(1)(A) (21 U.S.C. 355(b)(1)(A)) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act 53 (FD&C Act) requires, among other things, that an NDA include “a full list of the articles used as 54 components of such drug” and “a full statement of the composition of such drug.” 6 Further, 21 55 CFR 314.50(d)(1)(ii)( a ) requires that an NDA contains a “list of all components used in the 56 manufacture of the drug product (regardless of whether they appear in the drug product) and a 57 statement of the composition of the drug product.” 58 4 For more information on the eCTD format, see https://www.fda.gov/drugs/electronic-regulatory-submission-and- review/electronic-common-technical-document-ectd .

candidates.statement: The ANDA applicant is required to identify and characterize the inactive ingredients, 11 so FDA 71 can determine whether such inactive ingredients affect the safety or efficacy of the proposed 72 drug product. 12 Certain drug products (i.e., parenteral, ophthalmic, and otic routes of 73 administration) must have the same inactive ingredients (i.e., Q1 sameness) in the same 74 concentration (i.e., Q2 sameness), with exceptions, to ensure the inactive ingredients do not 75 affect the drug product’s safety or efficacy. 13 Certain drug products’ bioequivalence (BE) may 76 be deemed self-evident if the drug product has the same inactive ingredients in the same 77 concentration as a drug product that is the subject of an approved NDA or ANDA. 14

candidates.statement: Generally, the statement of ingredients in the approved labeling should be qualitatively and 110 quantitatively consistent with the composition statement in section 3.2.P.1 of the eCTD. 111 Applicants of nonoral use drugs must disclose the names of all inactive ingredients and, for 112 certain drug products, the quantities in the labeling. 19 In addition, qualitative information 113 required by 21 CFR 201.100(b)(5), such as the identity and effect of tonicity agents or pH 114 adjusters, must be listed in the approved labeling. In these situations, applicants should declare 115 the names of pH adjusters in the labeling statement per 21 CFR 201.100(b)(5)(iii). 116

candidates.statement: Applicants should ensure drug product composition statements are qualitatively and 134 quantitatively consistent throughout the entire application. The composition statement submitted 135 in section 3.2.P.1 is the composition that should be used throughout the application. Generally, 136 any submission that has a composition statement (e.g., addition of new colors or flavors, 137 modification of inactive ingredient levels, changes in inactive ingredient grades) that differs from 138 the composition statement submitted in section 3.2.P.1 should be accompanied by a composition 139 table in section 3.2.P.1, and FDA would consider this a change in formulation. Any supplements 140 that discuss drug product composition should be identical to the submitted section 3.2.P.1 and 141 contain a statement that section 3.2.P.1 has not changed. If an applicant does wish to submit 142 changes to a composition statement, the applicant should submit an amendment to section 143 3.2.P.1. 20
candidates.context: B. Consistency in Compositions Identified Within the Same Application 132 1. Consistency Between the Composition Statement and the Master Batch or 146 Executed Batch Records 147

candidates.statement: Applicants should ensure drug product composition statements are qualitatively and 149 quantitatively consistent throughout the application including, but not limited to, the composition 150 table in section 3.2.P.1, batch formula in section 3.2.P.3.2, and the executed and master 151 production (blank manufacturing) records in section 3.2.R. 152
candidates.context: 1. Consistency Between the Composition Statement and the Master Batch or 146 Executed Batch Records 147 Example 1: The drug product composition table in section 3.2.P.1 does not list any pH 154 adjusters. However, the drug product batch formula in section 3.2.P.3.2 lists a strong acid and 155 strong base as pH adjusters. The executed batch records also indicate the use of both types of pH 156 adjusters. In this case, the composition statement in section 3.2.P.1 does not accurately reflect 157 the drug product information, and the applicant should revise the composition statement to 158 include the acid and base components. 159

Clear Identification of Components of Inactive Ingredients 185

candidates.statement: Applicants should clearly identify components of inactive ingredients. An example of a failure 187 to clearly identify components is when an applicant does not include a drug master file (DMF) 188 with a selected source that contains an active ingredient with multiple components. FDA 189 encourages applicants to identify a DMF along with a letter of authorization to reference the 190 DMF or provide the components of the mixture and their amounts in the application. References 191 to DMFs should clearly identify the DMF number and location (e.g., page number) of the 192 relevant component composition information. The DMF should contain information about 193 components of inactive ingredient mixtures such as colorant, flavor, essence, or materials used in 194 their preparation. 21
candidates.context: 3. Clear Identification of Components of Inactive Ingredients 185 A further example of when an inactive ingredient may not be clearly identified is when an 197 inactive ingredient name or United States Pharmacopeia (USP)-National Formulary (NF) title in 198 the composition statement does not identify a single substance but refers to a family or drug 199 product line with different chemical structures (e.g., hypromellose). In such cases, the 200 composition statement is incomplete unless the applicant specifies the inactive ingredient grade 201 or type 22 that fully identifies the inactive ingredient composition (e.g., hypromellose 2910 (with 202 specified millipascal second). 23

candidates.statement: An applicant should clearly list units of measure for the quantity or concentration of inactive 218 ingredients in a composition statement (e.g., weight per weight (w/w) percent; weight per 219 volume (w/v) percent; volume per volume (v/v) percent). Applicants sometimes erroneously list 220 quantities in composition statements in different units of measure without noting the change in 221 units from the other inactive ingredients in the composition. Instead, FDA recommends that 222 applicants use the same units of concentration for all inactive ingredients, where appropriate, and 223 include additional information, such as ingredient and/or inactive ingredient density, used in the 224 calculations to convert the inactive ingredient concentration units. Where applicable, applicants 225 should show the calculations for such conversions. FDA recommends that applicants clearly 226 denote the difference in concentration units for those inactive ingredients and any associated 227 justification for the difference. 228

candidates.statement: Applicants should indicate in the composition table whether the amount or concentration listed 265 for the inactive ingredient represents the anhydrous amount, where applicable (also sometimes 266 known as the dehydrate (i.e., dried) amount). When using an anhydrous ingredient, applicants 267 should refer to the ingredient as anhydrous , not dehydrate , to avoid confusion with the term 268 dihydrate . Anhydrous and dihydrate terms are consistent with USP-NF monograph terminology. 269 Additionally, applicants should specify which grade or type of the inactive ingredient is used, 270 where applicable (see section III.C.4, Correct Nomenclature in Composition Statements and in 271 Applications Statements of Ingredients in Labeling). 272

candidates.statement: If an applicant lists multiple functions for an inactive ingredient, the applicant should indicate the 276 primary function of the ingredient in the proposed drug product in its application. candidates.statement: Applicants should clearly identify the functionality of an inactive ingredient in their applications. 283 The functionality of an inactive ingredient should describe the role of the ingredient in the 284 formulation as opposed to the mechanistic action of the ingredient. For example, chelating agent 285 describes the mechanism by which the ingredient binds metal ions, but does not describe the 286 actual function, or role, such as preservative or antioxidant, of the ingredient in the formulation. 287
candidates.context: 3. Clarity Regarding Functionality of Inactive Ingredients 281 Applicants should refrain from using ambiguous terminology when identifying the functionality 289 of inactive ingredients in their applications. Examples of ambiguous terminology include, but 290 are not limited to, the following: pH buffering agent , acidifying agent , and alkalizing agent . 291 Instead of pH buffering agent , applicants should simply use the term buffering agent when the 292 ingredient acts with a conjugate acid or base to buffer the composition from changes to the pH. 293 When the primary function of an inactive ingredient is to alter the pH of the formulation and is 294 commonly a strong acid or base, the ingredient’s primary function should be listed as a pH 295 adjuster . candidates.statement: Applicants should use the Global Substance Registration System (GSRS) display name, which 308 identifies the Unique Ingredient Identifiers for a particular inactive ingredient, in the composition 309 statement. If the GSRS preferred term differs from the USP-NF monograph title, FDA 310 recommends adding the USP monograph title with an asterisk below the composition statement 311 for clarity and to demonstrate consistency with the labeled statement of ingredients. See 312 Appendix for an example. Applicants should list the ingredients’ hydration state(s) and provide 313 additional relevant descriptive information, as appropriate. 26 Additionally, if the inactive 314 ingredient has multiple hydration states and is the subject of a USP monograph, applicants 315 should use a footnote to provide the inactive ingredient’s USP monograph title and equivalent 316 amount based on the monograph definition. Furthermore, when an inactive ingredient has 317 multiple hydration states, the USP monograph definition explains how those quantities should be 318 expressed. Where use of the inactive ingredient in a composition statement deviates from the 319 USP monograph, applicants should provide a statement that describes the deviation. 27

candidates.statement: In an annual report, applicants may make minor editorial changes (e.g., correcting a 336 typographical error) that do not affect the actual drug product composition, or they may delete or 337 reduce an ingredient intended to affect only the color of the drug product. 33 Generally, changes 338 to a composition statement that go beyond those listed at 21 CFR 314.70(d) would not fall into 339 either of these categories. In these circumstances, applicants should submit updated composition 340 statements in a submission after approval. 341
